extracted.intended_audience: patent owners, patent litigators, IP attorneys, and clients seeking guidance on proving lost-profits damages
extracted.subtask_description: Practical/legal guidance for proving and calculating lost-profits damages in patent-infringement cases, centered on the Panduit four-factor causation test and accepted accounting methods for damages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forms of lost profits
rubrics_metrics.description: "Lost profits may take the form of diverted sales, eroded prices, or increased expenses."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This describes the types of injury that lost-profits damages can cover — lost unit sales diverted to the infringer, reductions in price the patentee had to accept (price erosion), and extra costs the patentee incurred because of the infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causation: 'but for' requirement and burden
rubrics_metrics.description: "The burden rests on the patentee to show a reasonable probability that 'but for' the infringing activity, the patentee would have made the infringer’s sales."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patentee must reconstruct a hypothetical market as it would have existed absent the infringing product; causation must be supported by sound economic proof. Once the patentee meets the inference of causation (e.g., by satisfying the Panduit factors), the burden shifts to the infringer to show the inference is unreasonable for some or all infringing sales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panduit Factor 1 — Demand for the patented product
rubrics_metrics.description: To satisfy Panduit Factor 1, the patentee must show "demand for the patented product." The first factor "considers demand for the product as a whole," while the second factor considers demand for particular limitations or features of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patentee may use any relevant evidence to show demand, including sales of embodying products, the accused infringer’s decision to continue selling despite risk of infringement, and the patented feature's promotion or significance. Sales of the infringing product can be used but may require showing comparable sales prices; if products are not sufficiently similar, customers might not transfer demand. The inquiry ties damages to specific claim limitations to ensure forfeits are commensurate with value of patented features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panduit Factor 2 — Absence of acceptable, non-infringing alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Patentee must show a lack of acceptable, non-infringing alternatives: the alternative was either not acceptable to customers or not available at the time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acceptability compares the alternative to the patentee’s product (not just whether it could replace the infringing product). Availability is judged for the relevant accounting period (period of infringement claimed). If a substitute was not on the market during the accounting period, it may be inferred unavailable, and the accused infringer bears the burden to show availability. Any alternative proffered by the infringer must also be non-infringing; the patentee may challenge this and bear some burden to show infringement of the alternative. Mere existence of a competing product does not make it acceptable. In elastic markets, an alleged alternative must not be disparately higher priced or have significantly different characteristics; in inelastic markets greater price disparity can be acceptable if the patentee demonstrates market inelasticity and adjusts analysis accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Market-share theory as an alternative to proving no acceptable substitute
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentee may meet Panduit Factor 2 under a market-share theory: lost profits may be awarded "if the patentee shows an established market share in lieu of the absence of acceptable noninfringing alternatives and, at the same time, meets the three other Panduit factors."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have relied on evidence such as past business practices investing in market development, testimony about loss of business and prior customer relationships, head-to-head competition, real sales losses, and national recognition to support market-share claims. Market-share theory requires demonstrating an established market position plus the other Panduit factors (demand, ability to meet demand, amount of profits).

rubrics_metrics.name: Panduit Factor 3 — Ability to meet demand (manufacturing/marketing capability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patentee must demonstrate it had the manufacturing capabilities to exploit the demand represented by the infringing sales — i.e., capacity to absorb the market share of the infringing sales during the period of infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence can include past business practices and relationships, sales reports, financial strength, efforts to develop a market, aggressiveness in the market, market competition, lost sales, testimony regarding prior sales activities, and national recognition. Lost profits are generally unavailable if the patentee did not sell or seek to sell the patented product or a marketable substitute in the United States, though in rare circumstances (e.g., driven from the market by infringement) a patentee who did not sell during the damages period may still recover if demand can be shown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panduit Factor 4 — Amount of profits patentee would have made
rubrics_metrics.description: Patentee must prove the amount of profits it would have made but for the infringement. The supporting calculation does not require exact precision, only "that there was a reasonable probability that the infringing sales caused the loss of profits."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any doubts about calculatory precision are resolved against the infringer. Lost profits can include diverted sales, price erosion, and increased expenditures caused by infringement. Once the patentee establishes the reasonableness of the inference, the onus is on the infringer to show it is unreasonable to infer some or all infringing sales caused the loss.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calculation method: Incremental income / gross margin approach
rubrics_metrics.description: The incremental income (gross margin) approach is an accepted method: it recognizes that producing unit N+1 does not cost as much if initial units already paid fixed costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under this approach, fixed costs (costs not varying with production increases, such as management salaries, property taxes, insurance) are excluded when determining profits. The page cites supporting authorities and indicates this method is well established in patent-damages law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible evidence and burden-shifting notes
rubrics_metrics.description: Various types of evidence can be used across factors (e.g., sales of embodying products, accused infringer's continued sales despite risk, promotion/significance of patented feature, sales reports, financial strength, past customer relationships, head-to-head competition, testimony regarding lost business).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The patentee may rely on these types of evidence to prove demand, absence of acceptable substitutes, ability to meet demand, and loss amount. Courts treat some elements as questions of fact (amount of lost profits, absence of acceptable substitutes) and recognize inferences (e.g., when patentee and infringer were the only suppliers). When inferences arise, the accused infringer may rebut by showing availability of substitutes or that the inference is unreasonable.
